match.reason: The bank point covers drafting, revising and editing at a basic level, but it does not cover getting feedback or explaining why changes were made, and its depth is lower than a Year 11 VCE Units 1 and 2 point needs.

draft.title: Drafting and refining
card: Draft
a first version of a piece. It gets ideas onto the page and does not need to be perfect.
Feedback
comments from a teacher or peer on how well the piece works for its purpose and audience.
Revise
change bigger things, such as structure, order of ideas, or what to add or cut.
Polish
fix smaller things, such as word choice, sentence flow, spelling and punctuation. A writer can explain why each change was made.
draft.remember: Draft, get feedback, revise the big things, polish the small ones, and know why you changed each.

a.q: Which change is an example of revising rather than polishing?
opts: Moving the strongest scene to the start of the story
Swapping 'big' for a more exact word
Fixing a missing comma in one sentence
Correcting the spelling of a character's name
a.why: Moving a scene changes the structure, which is revising. Swapping a word is tempting, but word choice and small fixes are polishing.
a.clue: Which change affects the order of the whole piece?

b.q: Omar's peer says his speech's main point appears too late. He moves it to the opening and explains that listeners need it early. What has Omar done?
opts: Revised the structure and given a reason for it
Polished the spelling and punctuation of the speech
Written a first draft of the speech
Ignored the feedback to keep his original plan
b.why: Moving the main point changes structure, so it is revision, and Omar explained why. It is not polishing because no small language fixes were made.
b.clue: Was the change big or small, and did he give a reason?

a.best: Moving the strongest scene to the start of the story

b.best: Revised the structure and given a reason for it

proposal.title: Drafting and refining
card: A draft is a first version of a piece. It gets ideas onto the page and does not need to be perfect. Feedback is comments from a teacher or peer on how well it works for its purpose and audience.
Revise
change bigger things, such as the structure, the order of ideas, or what to add or cut.
Polish
fix smaller things, such as word choice, sentence flow, spelling and punctuation.
Whether a change is big or small, a writer can explain why they made it and how it helps the piece.
proposal.remember: Revise the big things, polish the small ones, and be able to say why you changed each.

a.q: Which change is an example of revising rather than polishing?
opts: Cutting a scene that slows down the middle of the story
Swapping 'walked' for 'trudged' in the opening scene
Adding a missing comma to a line in the final scene
Fixing the spelling of a name in the second scene
a.why: Cutting a whole scene changes what the piece contains, which is revising. Swapping in a more exact word is tempting, but word choice is a small change, so it is polishing.
a.clue: Think about how much of the piece each change affects.

b.q: Omar's peer says his speech's main point appears too late. He moves it to the opening and explains that listeners need it early. What has Omar done?
opts: Revised the structure and given a reason for it
Polished the wording and given a reason for it
Written a first draft and given a reason for it
Ignored the feedback and kept his original order
b.why: Moving the main point changes the structure, so it is revision, and Omar explained why. It is not polishing, because he changed the order of ideas rather than the wording of sentences.
b.clue: Was the change to the order of ideas or to the words?
